The 2018 edition forbids tripping inside the continuous operation region of 0.88 to 1.10 pu, requires ride-through under three abnormal operating performance categories (Category III's default undervoltage trip is 0.88 pu at 21 seconds against Category I's 0.88 pu at 2 seconds), harmonises frequency ride-through with continuous operation from 58.8 to 61.2 Hz and mandatory operation down to 57.0 Hz and up to 62.0 Hz for 299 seconds, and requires dynamic reactive power support. Default frequency trips are 62.0 Hz at 0.16 s, 61.2 Hz at 300 s, 58.5 Hz at 300 s and 56.5 Hz at 0.16 s. Conformance is tested to IEEE 1547.1-2020.
standards.why: It is the single standard that decides whether a high-renewables distribution grid is stable or is a machine for turning small faults into big ones. The 2016 Blue Cut Fire event saw roughly 1200 MW of California solar disconnect from one fault, under the old rules, working as designed.
standards.gameEffect: The most legible grid mechanic in the set. Inverters compliant with IEEE 1547-2018 ride through a voltage dip instead of disconnecting, so a cloud passing over the solar district or a fault two feeders away no longer browns out the hospital. Build a district on 1547-2003 legacy inverters and any fault event drops every DER on that feeder for 5 minutes of game time, cascading into load shedding once DER penetration passes about 20 percent. Category selection is a real choice the player makes per feeder: Category III keeps generation online through disturbances but raises the anti-islanding risk that endangers line crews during repair, so it costs longer outage-repair times; Category I is safer to work on and less stable. Retrofitting a district's inverters to 1547-2018 is a mid-game capital project with an immediately visible reliability jump.

standards.title: IEEE Standard for Smart Energy Profile Application Protocol
standards.bodyFull: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, Standards Association
standards.edition: 2023 revision of the 2018 edition, with corrigendum incorporated; status confirmed Active on the IEEE SA record 2026-08-09
standards.what: The application-layer protocol a utility uses to talk to equipment behind the customer's meter: demand response, load control, time-of-day pricing, distributed generation management and EV charging. It is RESTful over TCP/IP and HTTP, draws its information model from IEC 61968 and IEC 61850, and is explicitly built to support everything IEEE 1547-2018 requires. California Rule 21 made it the default communication requirement for smart inverters, which is what drove adoption. The 2023 revision keeps backward compatibility with 2018 except that mandatory DERControl modes were removed, and adds EV charging function sets and refined DER monitoring.
standards.why: IEEE 1547 says what an inverter must be able to do. Without a common protocol to tell it to do that, the capability sits unused, and a grid full of capable-but-uncommanded inverters is no better than a grid full of dumb ones.
standards.gameEffect: Unlocks active grid management as a playable layer rather than a passive stat. With 2030.5 deployed, the player can dispatch distributed resources: curtail rooftop solar during a reverse-power event, discharge home batteries into the evening peak, shift EV charging off the peak. Each dispatched megawatt of flexibility substitutes for a megawatt of peaker plant. Without it, all that capacity exists on the map and cannot be called, and the player must build generation for the peak instead. Deploying it is a per-district communications upgrade with a modest cost and a long install time.

standards.title: Communication networks and systems for power utility automation
standards.bodyFull: International Electrotechnical Commission, technical committee TC 57
standards.edition: A multi-part series; the IEC webstore carries the series entry as IEC 61850:2026 SER, with parts at individual editions. IEC 61850-7-420:2021 (Edition 2.0) covers distributed energy resources
standards.what: The standard that let substation equipment from different vendors talk to each other. Before it, every protection relay spoke its manufacturer's protocol and integrating a substation was a bespoke engineering project. It defines an abstract data model of logical nodes and common data classes, maps it onto real protocols, and adds a machine-readable Substation Configuration Language (Part 6) so a substation design is a file rather than folklore. GOOSE messages run at Ethernet layer 2, bypassing TCP/IP, for fast protection and interlocking between intelligent electronic devices; Sampled Measured Values digitise current and voltage on the process bus, replacing copper instrument-transformer wiring. Part 7-420 (2021) extends the model to distributed generation, storage, controllable loads, microgrid energy management and distribution automation, and is explicitly built to represent the grid-code functions of IEEE 1547, EN 50549 and IEC 62786 in one common model.
standards.why: A city that has to buy every future substation from the same vendor as its first one is locked in for forty years. Interoperability is what keeps the upgrade path open, and the upgrade path is what lets the grid change fast enough.
standards.gameEffect: Substations built to IEC 61850 accept components from any manufacturer and can be upgraded incrementally; proprietary substations lock the player to one supplier, whose prices rise 10 percent each decade and whose product line can be discontinued as a mid-game event, forcing a full and expensive replacement. GOOSE-enabled protection clears faults in milliseconds instead of hundreds of milliseconds, shrinking the blast radius of a fault from a district to a feeder. Part 7-420 is the prerequisite that lets the DER dispatch of IEEE 2030.5 actually reach the substation control layer.

standards.title: Industrial communication networks - Network and system security - Part 3-3: System security requirements and security levels
standards.bodyFull: International Electrotechnical Commission, developed jointly with the International Society of Automation (ISA/IEC 62443)
standards.edition: Edition 1.0, 2013-08, with corrigendum (2014-04) incorporated
standards.what: The system-level technical security requirements for industrial automation and control systems, organised under seven foundational requirements: identification and authentication control, use control, system integrity, data confidentiality, restricted data flow, timely response to events, and resource availability. Each requirement has a base form plus optional enhancements mapped to a security level. The levels run SL 0 (no specific requirement), SL 1 (casual or accidental misuse), SL 2 (intentional misuse with simple means and low motivation), SL 3 (sophisticated means, moderate resources, control-system-specific knowledge), SL 4 (sophisticated means, extensive resources, high motivation). A level is not one number but a vector of seven, one per foundational requirement, and it comes in three flavours: SL-C the capability a system has, SL-T the target a zone needs, and SL-A what was achieved. Assignment runs through IEC 62443-3-2: split the plant into zones and conduits, run a risk assessment, set a target per zone. The community's own literature admits no vetted way to quantify a level has been developed.
standards.why: A modern grid is a control system with a power plant attached. Ukraine 2015 and 2016 showed that turning a city's lights off is now a software operation, and the zone-and-conduit model is the architecture that limits how far an intruder gets.
standards.gameEffect: Sets the cyberattack model. The player assigns a target security level per zone (generation control, substation automation, distribution SCADA, metering) and pays for it. Attack events arrive with an attacker sophistication that maps directly onto the SL scale: an SL 1 zone falls to a commodity attack, an SL 3 zone stops a state-adjacent actor. The zone-and-conduit split is what actually matters mechanically: a flat network loses everything to one breach, while a properly segmented grid loses only the zone that was hit. Under-specifying one zone creates the weak conduit that lets an attacker walk from the office network to the substation.

standards.title: Security for industrial automation and control systems - Part 2-1: Security program requirements for IACS asset owners
standards.bodyFull: International Electrotechnical Commission, developed jointly with the International Society of Automation
standards.edition: Edition 2.0, 2024-08. Supersedes the 2010 first edition
standards.what: The obligations on the ASSET OWNER, as distinct from the vendor: what a utility operating a control system has to have in place as an ongoing programme, not as a one-time build. Edition 2 reorganised the requirements around Security Program Elements, deliberately harmonised them with ISO/IEC 27001 so an operator is not running two parallel management systems, and added a four-level maturity model: Initial, Managed, Defined, Improving. The distinction between this and Part 3-3 is the distinction between having secure equipment and running it securely, and it is the second one that usually fails.
standards.why: Almost every real utility intrusion succeeded against equipment that was technically capable of stopping it. The gap is operational, and this is the standard that addresses the gap.
standards.gameEffect: A recurring operating cost with a maturity track, not a one-off purchase. The player funds a security programme at one of four maturity levels; the level decays if funding is cut, which models the real failure mode of security spending. Maturity multiplies the effective security level of every zone: an SL 3 zone run by an Initial-maturity organisation behaves as SL 2 under attack, while an Improving-maturity organisation gets a bonus detection roll. It also governs incident recovery time: a mature programme restores a compromised substation in hours, an immature one in days.

standards.title: NERC Critical Infrastructure Protection Reliability Standards (CIP-002 through CIP-015)
standards.bodyFull: North American Electric Reliability Corporation, the Electric Reliability Organization designated by FERC under the Energy Policy Act of 2005
standards.edition: A family of standards on independent revision cycles; the newest member is CIP-015-1, effective 2025-09-02
standards.what: The mandatory and enforceable cyber and physical security standards for the North American bulk electric system, with financial penalties for non-compliance. The family runs from CIP-002 (categorising bulk electric system cyber systems as high, medium or low impact) through CIP-003 security management, CIP-004 personnel and training, CIP-005 electronic security perimeters, CIP-006 physical security of cyber systems, CIP-007 system security management, CIP-008 incident reporting, CIP-009 recovery plans, CIP-010 configuration change management, CIP-011 information protection, CIP-013 supply chain risk management, CIP-014 physical security of critical transmission stations, to CIP-015 internal network security monitoring. CIP-015-1 is the newest and the most interesting: approved by FERC in Order No. 907 (2025-06-26), effective 2025-09-02, it requires collection of east-west traffic INSIDE the electronic security perimeter, because every earlier control watched the fence and attacks that matter get in and then move sideways. Compliance is due 2028-10-01 for high and medium impact systems with external routable connectivity and 2030-10-01 for the rest.
standards.why: This is the only material on this page that is mandatory on its own terms rather than voluntary-until-adopted, and it is the reason a North American grid operator's security posture is a legal question rather than a budget question.
standards.gameEffect: A compliance regime rather than an upgrade. Once the player's grid crosses the bulk-system registration threshold, CIP applies automatically: an audit fires periodically, and gaps cost money in penalties and reputation rather than causing an outage directly. CIP-002 categorisation is a real decision, because classifying an asset as high impact triggers the full expensive control set and mis-classifying downward to save money is discovered at audit. CIP-015 internal monitoring changes attack resolution: without it a breach is detected only when something breaks, with it there is a detection roll during lateral movement that can stop an attack before it reaches generation control.

standards.title: Frequency and Voltage Ride-through Requirements for Inverter-Based Resources
standards.bodyFull: North American Electric Reliability Corporation
standards.edition: Approved by FERC in Order No. 909, July 2025. Effective 2026-10-01 for bulk electric system facilities; non-BES inverter-based resources from January 2027
standards.what: Mandatory frequency and voltage ride-through performance for inverter-based resources on the bulk power system: wind farms, utility-scale solar and grid batteries must inject current and provide voltage support during a disturbance, and momentary cessation is prohibited within the defined no-trip zone. Two things distinguish it from IEEE 1547. First, it is enforceable with penalties rather than adopted by reference. Second, and more interesting, compliance is demonstrated by BEHAVIOUR, not by settings: documenting that the correct values are configured does not discharge the obligation, and the resource's actual response during real grid events is the benchmark. PRC-028 provides the disturbance monitoring equipment that makes that demonstrable and PRC-030 covers reporting of ride-through failures. It exists because NERC's own event analyses documented repeated widespread ride-through failures, and FERC Order 901 directed it into being.
standards.why: The bulk system used to be held up by the physical inertia of spinning turbines. As that is replaced by inverters, the system's stability becomes a property of software settings, and this is the standard that makes those settings a legal obligation rather than a vendor default.
standards.gameEffect: Applies to utility-scale generation, where IEEE 1547 applies to distribution-connected. Once inverter-based resources exceed about 30 percent of the player's generation mix, a grid disturbance event triggers a system-wide ride-through check: PRC-029 compliant fleets stay online and the frequency recovers, non-compliant fleets trip together and the game runs a cascading-outage resolution that can black out the whole map. The behaviour-not-settings rule is modelled directly: the player must fund disturbance monitoring (PRC-028) to prove compliance, and a fleet that has never been through a real event carries an unverified flag that is resolved, expensively or well, the first time a disturbance hits.

standards.title: Voltage characteristics of electricity supplied by public electricity networks
standards.bodyFull: European Committee for Electrotechnical Standardization
standards.edition: 2022 edition, approved 2022-11-07, superseding EN 50160:2010 and amendments A1:2015, A2:2019, A3:2019; further amended by EN 50160:2022/A1:2025
standards.what: What the network operator owes the customer at the socket, under normal operating conditions, for public low voltage (up to 1 kV), medium (1 to 36 kV), high (36 to 150 kV) and extra-high voltage (150 to 800 kV). It covers frequency, magnitude, waveform (harmonics and flicker) and symmetry, measured per EN 61000-4-30. The frequency numbers, taken as the mean of the fundamental over a 10-second window: on a synchronously interconnected system, 50 Hz plus or minus 1 percent (49.5 to 50.5 Hz) for 99.5 percent of a year, and 50 Hz plus 4 percent minus 6 percent (47 to 52 Hz) for 100 percent of the time. On an islanded system the bands widen enormously, to plus or minus 2 percent for 95 percent of a week and plus or minus 15 percent (42.5 to 57.5 Hz) for 100 percent of the time. For low-voltage magnitude, nominal is 230 V and 95 percent of the 10-minute mean RMS values in each week must fall within plus or minus 10 percent, which is 207 to 253 V.
standards.why: The 99.5 percent allowance means frequency may legally sit outside the tight band for about 44 hours a year, and the islanded band being fifteen times wider than the interconnected one is the physical reason a small island grid is a harder engineering problem: there is no inertia to borrow.
standards.gameEffect: The power quality scoreboard, visible per district. Frequency and voltage are simulated against these bands and excursions are counted; exceed the 99.5 percent allowance and the player pays regulatory penalties and loses sensitive industrial and data-centre tenants, who relocate. It also creates the islanding trade-off: a microgrid that disconnects from the main network keeps the lights on during a regional outage but immediately falls under the wide islanded band, so precision manufacturing inside it shuts down anyway unless the player has built enough synchronous condensers or grid-forming inverters to hold frequency. Choosing between a hard island and a weak connection becomes a real decision.

standards.title: Commission Regulation establishing a network code on requirements for grid connection of generators (NC RfG)
standards.bodyFull: European Commission, network code drafted by ENTSO-E (European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity)
standards.edition: Adopted 14 April 2016, published in OJ L 112, 27.4.2016, pages 1 to 68
standards.what: Not a standard but a binding EU regulation, directly applicable in every Member State and prevailing over national provisions, though more detailed or more stringent compatible national codes still apply. It sets the capabilities a generating facility must have to connect: frequency and voltage ranges within which it must stay connected, fault ride-through, active power control and frequency response, reactive power capability, and the control and information interfaces. Requirements scale by type A, B, C and D, banded by connection voltage and capacity, so a rooftop inverter and a gas turbine are not held to the same rules. Two sibling codes cover demand connection (Regulation (EU) 2016/1388) and HVDC (Regulation (EU) 2016/1447). Article 58 obliges ENTSO-E to maintain non-binding Implementation Guidance Documents every two years with mandatory stakeholder consultation, and Article 7 requires any amendment to respect the legitimate expectations of facility owners and equipment manufacturers, a rule that exists because retroactive grid code changes strand hardware.
standards.why: It is the European answer to the same question IEEE 1547 answers in North America, and the fact that Europe answered it with law and North America answered it with a voluntary standard adopted state by state is the single clearest illustration of how differently the two systems govern their grids.
standards.gameEffect: The European map's connection gate. Every generator carries a type (A, B, C or D) set by its capacity and connection voltage, and each type unlocks a different requirement set the player must pay for: type A is trivial, type D demands full fault ride-through, reactive capability and remote control. Unlike the North American map, this is not optional and there is no cheap non-compliant build; the cost is front-loaded into every generator instead of arriving later as a reliability penalty. The trade is legible and worth teaching: the European grid costs more per megawatt installed and suffers fewer cascading events.

standards.title: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (Revised Edition)
standards.bodyFull: Greenhouse Gas Protocol, a partnership of the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD)
standards.edition: Revised Edition, 2004, revising the 2001 original
standards.what: The rulebook essentially every corporate emissions figure in the world is built on, and the document that invented SCOPES. Scope 1 is direct emissions from sources the organisation owns or controls. Scope 2 is indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heat and cooling. Scope 3 is every other indirect emission across the value chain. It also sets the organisational boundary choice (equity share, financial control or operational control) and the base-year recalculation rules, which is why an emissions figure can move because a company sold a subsidiary rather than because it emitted less. It is not an ISO standard, carries no ISO edition number and is certified by nobody; its authority is that everyone adopted it. Mandatory regimes that reference it include IFRS S2, the EU ESRS and California SB 253. It is currently under revision, with GHG Protocol and ISO working toward a unified corporate accounting framework.
standards.why: Every city climate plan, every corporate target and every disclosure regime rests on this one set of definitions, so the definitions are load-bearing infrastructure that most people using them have never read.
standards.gameEffect: Turns the emissions counter from a single number into three, and that split is the game. Scope 1 is what the city's own operations burn and the player controls directly. Scope 2 is the grid, which the player controls by changing the generation mix. Scope 3 is everything the city buys, which the player can only influence through procurement policy and which is usually the largest. Adopting the Corporate Standard reveals the three-way breakdown; without it the player sees one aggregate number and cannot tell which lever moves it. Boundary choice is a real decision: operational control excludes a jointly owned power plant that equity share would include, and picking the flattering boundary is available and is caught by the assurance mechanic.

standards.title: GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance: An amendment to the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard
standards.bodyFull: Greenhouse Gas Protocol (WRI and WBCSD)
standards.edition: 2015, under public consultation for revision since 2025-10-20 (consultation closed 2026-01-31); second consultation planned 2026, final publication expected 2027
standards.what: The most contested rulebook in corporate climate accounting. It requires DUAL reporting of purchased electricity emissions: a location-based figure using the average emissions intensity of the grid you physically draw from, and a market-based figure using the attributes of the contractual instruments you bought (renewable energy certificates, guarantees of origin, power purchase agreements, supplier-specific rates). The two can differ by an order of magnitude for the same electrons, and the market-based number is the one that goes on the front of the report. Annual, unbundled certificate matching is what lets a company claim 100 percent renewable electricity while drawing from a coal-heavy grid at three in the morning. The 2025 to 2026 revision proposes keeping dual reporting but adding hourly matching, a deliverability requirement and new emission factor rules for the market-based method, plus a tightened factor hierarchy for the location-based one. Consultation feedback showed very low support for mandatory hourly matching. The market-based approach is credited with adding more than 100 GW of clean electricity to the US grid since 2014.
standards.why: This is where most greenwashing lives, and it is also where most of the voluntary corporate clean-energy procurement of the last decade came from. Both statements are true, which is exactly why the revision is hard.
standards.gameEffect: Two emissions numbers, tracked side by side and both shown. The player can buy unbundled certificates cheaply and watch the market-based number fall while the location-based number does not move at all, and the game shows the divergence as a visible gap. Public trust and the disclosure score key off the LOCATION-based figure, so certificate-buying flatters the headline and does nothing for the city. Hourly matching is an unlockable stricter mode: procure generation that matches consumption hour by hour and the two numbers converge, which costs far more and actually decarbonises the grid the city sits on. Teaching that gap is the point of the mechanic.

standards.title: Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard
standards.bodyFull: Greenhouse Gas Protocol (WRI and WBCSD)
standards.edition: 2011; a public consultation draft of the revision is due in the second half of 2026
standards.what: Divides the value chain into 15 categories: eight upstream (purchased goods and services, capital goods, fuel and energy related activities not in Scope 1 or 2, upstream transport and distribution, waste generated in operations, business travel, employee commuting, upstream leased assets) and seven downstream (downstream transport and distribution, processing of sold products, use of sold products, end-of-life treatment of sold products, downstream leased assets, franchises, investments). For most organisations Scope 3 is the overwhelming majority of the footprint and the least certain part of it. Category 15, investments, is where a bank's financed emissions live and is usually larger than everything else the bank does combined.
standards.why: A city that counts only what it burns inside its boundary can decarbonise on paper by importing everything, and the Scope 3 categories are the machinery that makes that visible.
standards.gameEffect: Unlocks supply-chain emissions as a playable layer. Once adopted, every construction project, every imported good and every commuter journey attributes emissions to the city, and the player gains procurement policy as a lever: specify low-carbon concrete and steel, source food regionally, electrify the freight corridor. It also creates the honest trap: a city that offshores its industry sees Scope 1 fall and Scope 3 rise by more, and the total goes up. Without the Scope 3 standard adopted, that offshoring shows as a pure win, which is exactly the false lesson the mechanic exists to prevent.

standards.title: Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventories
standards.bodyFull: Greenhouse Gas Protocol, developed jointly by the World Resources Institute, C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group and ICLEI - Local Governments for Sustainability
standards.edition: Version 1.1, updating the 2014 original to align with the 2019 Refinement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines. Table 1.2 of the document lists every change
standards.what: THE city-level inventory standard, and the one a city builder should teach above all the others. It covers six sectors: stationary energy; transportation; waste; industrial processes and product use; agriculture, forestry and other land use; and other emissions outside the boundary. Cities report at one of two levels. BASIC covers Scope 1 and Scope 2 from stationary energy and transportation plus Scope 1 and Scope 3 from waste. BASIC+ adds the harder sources, notably transboundary journeys as Scope 3 transport, plus industrial processes and land use. The GPC is production-based: it counts what is emitted inside the boundary plus the grid energy imported, and it explicitly does NOT count emissions embodied in the goods and services the city consumes, which the standard itself says cities should address separately. It supersedes ICLEI's 2009 community protocol and the 2010 World Bank, UNEP and UN-HABITAT city standard.
standards.why: This is how a city knows what it emitted, and the BASIC versus BASIC+ choice is the difference between an inventory a city can produce this year and one that is actually complete. The production-based boundary is the single most important caveat in municipal climate policy: a wealthy service city can post an excellent number while importing everything it uses from somewhere with a terrible one.
standards.gameEffect: The city's emissions ledger, and the thing every climate target in the game is scored against. Completing a BASIC inventory unlocks targets, climate finance and network membership; BASIC+ costs more staff time and reveals the transboundary transport and industrial emissions that BASIC hides, typically raising the reported total by 15 to 40 percent. That reveal is a deliberate and painful moment: the player's number goes UP because they measured better, and any target set against the BASIC figure has to be renegotiated. Adopting BASIC+ early is the harder and correct play.
standards.supersedes: ICLEI International Local Government GHG Emissions Analysis Protocol (2009), community section

standards.title: Greenhouse gases - Part 1: Specification with guidance at the organization level for quantification and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions and removals
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization, technical committee ISO/TC 207/SC 7
standards.edition: Edition 2, 2018, superseding the 2006 first edition. ISO record shows stage 90.92 with an amendment in progress (ISO 14064-1:2018/DAM 1:2024)
standards.what: The international-standard counterpart to the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard: requirements for designing, developing, managing, reporting and verifying an organisation's greenhouse gas inventory across direct and indirect emissions and removals. Its terminology differs from the GHG Protocol deliberately, speaking of direct emissions and indirect emissions in six categories rather than three scopes, which is a real interoperability friction and one of the things the ISO and GHG Protocol alignment work is meant to fix. A defining property of the whole ISO 14060 family is that it is programme-neutral: where a GHG programme applies, that programme's requirements are additional to the standard's.
standards.why: A number produced to an ISO standard can be accredited and verified through the ISO conformity assessment machinery, which is what a regulator or a court will recognise. The GHG Protocol number is more widely used; the ISO number is more defensible.
standards.gameEffect: The alternative accounting track to the GHG Protocol, and picking between them matters. ISO 14064-1 costs more to implement and produces a figure that can be verified to ISO 14064-3 by an accredited body, which unlocks regulated markets, public procurement eligibility and the higher tier of climate finance. The GHG Protocol route is cheaper and faster and is what the voluntary networks accept. A city that runs both pays twice and has to reconcile six categories against three scopes, which is a small ongoing administrative cost and an accurate depiction of what real organisations do.

standards.title: Greenhouse gases - Part 3: Specification with guidance for the verification and validation of greenhouse gas statements
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization, technical committee ISO/TC 207/SC 7
standards.edition: Edition 2, published 2019-04, 54 pages. Last reviewed and confirmed in 2024 (stage 90.93)
standards.what: The standard the independent assurer works to. It covers verification of historical greenhouse gas statements (organisational inventories, projects, product carbon footprints) and validation of forward-looking ones, and it is what turns 'we measured our emissions' into 'someone independent checked'. The distinction between REASONABLE assurance and LIMITED assurance lives here, and it is the distinction that decides whether a disclosure has actually been audited or merely reviewed: limited assurance is a negative-form conclusion (nothing came to our attention) at far lower cost and effort than reasonable assurance's positive opinion.
standards.why: Almost every mandatory disclosure regime is phasing in from limited to reasonable assurance, and the phase-in dates are among the most consequential lines in climate regulation, because they are when the numbers start having to survive an audit.
standards.gameEffect: The verification layer that makes every other accounting number trustworthy or not. Unverified figures carry a public-trust discount: investors, networks and the disclosure score apply a haircut. Limited assurance removes most of the discount at moderate cost. Reasonable assurance removes all of it and unlocks the highest tier of green financing, but is expensive and can FAIL, forcing a restatement that costs reputation badly. The mechanic makes the player choose between a cheap number nobody quite believes and an expensive one that can blow up if their inventory work was sloppy.

standards.title: Climate change management - Transition to net zero - Part 1: Carbon neutrality
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, November 2023, introduced at COP28
standards.what: The first International Standard for making a carbon neutrality claim. It specifies how to achieve and demonstrate carbon neutrality of a SUBJECT, which may be an organisation or a product including goods, services, events and buildings. Its central discipline is a mitigation hierarchy: direct and indirect emission reductions and removal enhancements WITHIN the value chain come first, and offsetting handles only the residue. It requires broader inclusion of material Scope 3 emissions than PAS 2060 did. It builds on ISO 14064-1, ISO 14064-3 and ISO 14067 and sits under the ISO Net Zero Guidelines launched at COP27. Two exclusions matter: territories such as cities are out of scope, and so is territorial emissions reporting to the UNFCCC, so a city cannot certify ITSELF neutral under this standard.
standards.why: Carbon neutrality claims were an unpoliced market until this existed. The mitigation hierarchy is the specific rule that makes buying your way to neutrality without reducing anything non-compliant.
standards.gameEffect: Governs whether the player's organisations may make neutrality claims and what those claims are worth. A claim backed by ISO 14068-1 verification requires the mitigation hierarchy to be demonstrated, so the game checks that actual reductions preceded offset purchases; a player who tries to offset first has the claim rejected and takes a greenwashing reputation hit. The exclusion of cities is a teaching moment made mechanical: the player CANNOT certify the city neutral under this standard and must use the GPC plus a validated target route instead, while individual municipal organisations and buildings can be certified.

standards.title: Specification for the demonstration of carbon neutrality
standards.bodyFull: British Standards Institution (a Publicly Available Specification, a BSI fast-track document rather than a full British Standard)
standards.edition: PAS 2060:2014, revising the 2010 original
standards.what: The document most carbon neutrality claims were made against for a decade, and it is now retired. BSI stopped delivering the PAS 2060:2014 verification scheme on 2025-01-01, and the document was withdrawn from use on 2025-11-30, at the end of the 24-month transition from the publication of ISO 14068-1:2023. BSI's ISO 14068-1 verification scheme has been available since 2024-03-01. Opinions previously issued against PAS 2060 remain valid for the historical periods they cover, so a claim about past neutrality can still cite it, but a FRESH neutrality claim verified to PAS 2060 is not valid. The substantive reason it was replaced: PAS 2060 did not enforce a reduction pathway before offsetting and allowed considerable latitude over which emissions to include, which left room to buy neutrality outright.
standards.why: It is in this list precisely because it is dead and is still cited as live by a great many corporate pages. Knowing that a familiar certification has been retired, and what replaced it, is a real piece of literacy.
standards.gameEffect: A legacy state rather than a build option. Organisations in the game world that were certified under PAS 2060 before the cutover keep their historical badge, but any attempt to renew fails and forces migration to ISO 14068-1, which costs money and can reveal that the old claim would not have passed the new mitigation hierarchy. A player who notices a partner still advertising PAS 2060 neutrality in 2026 can call it out for a small reputation gain, which is the standard teaching itself through play.

standards.title: SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard, Version 2.0
standards.bodyFull: Science Based Targets initiative, a partnership of CDP, the United Nations Global Compact, the World Resources Institute and WWF
standards.edition: Version 2.0, published 2026-06-11, the largest revision since the 2021 original
standards.what: Not a standard in the standards-body sense but a target-setting framework plus a validation service: a company submits targets, SBTi checks them against published criteria, and validated targets are published. There is no ISO or national accreditation behind it and its authority is entirely reputational, and it is enormous anyway. Version 2.0 introduces company categorisation by size AND jurisdiction income (Category A is large companies everywhere plus medium companies in high-income countries; Category B is small companies and medium companies in lower-income countries), SEPARATE Scope 1 and Scope 2 targets rather than a combined one, a 5 percent Scope 3 threshold, MANDATORY assurance, mandatory governance and board accountability and transition planning, expanded carbon-removal provisions, and a 'best efforts' recognition. The transition timetable is easy to get wrong: V1.3.1 remains the validation framework throughout 2026, either version may be submitted from Q1 2027, and V2.0 is mandatory from 2028-01-31. Existing validated targets stay valid through their cycle.
standards.why: It is the closest thing the world has to a referee on whether a company's climate target is serious, and V2.0's move to mandatory assurance and separate Scope 1 and 2 targets closes the two loopholes that let a target look good without changing operations.
standards.gameEffect: The target validation gate. The player sets a decarbonisation target for the city's own operations and its major partners; submitting it to SBTi either passes or is rejected with a reason, and only validated targets count for the disclosure score, green financing rate and network membership. The separate Scope 1 and Scope 2 targets matter mechanically: the old combined target could be met entirely by buying clean electricity while the city's own vehicle fleet and boilers went untouched, and V2.0 forbids that, forcing the player to actually electrify the fleet. Mandatory assurance means the target also costs an ongoing verification budget.

standards.title: General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information
standards.bodyFull: International Sustainability Standards Board, housed in the IFRS Foundation
standards.edition: Issued June 2023, effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024
standards.what: The umbrella standard for sustainability disclosure. It requires an entity to disclose material information about all the sustainability-related risks and opportunities that could reasonably be expected to affect its cash flows, its access to finance or its cost of capital over the short, medium or long term. Two requirements do most of the work and are the quiet radical part: the disclosure must be made AT THE SAME TIME as the financial statements, and it must cover the SAME reporting entity. That drags sustainability reporting out of the standalone glossy report and into the annual accounts, on the auditor's timetable and inside the auditor's scope.
standards.why: Everything before it was published whenever a company felt like it, covering whatever boundary flattered it best. Same time, same entity is what makes the numbers comparable and makes them assurable.
standards.gameEffect: Unlocks the disclosure track and sets its timing. Once adopted, the city's and its major partners' climate information must be published on the financial reporting calendar, so the player can no longer delay a bad year's numbers until they have improved. It also aligns the reporting boundary with the financial one, which closes the trick of excluding an inconveniently dirty subsidiary from the climate report while consolidating its profits.

standards.title: Climate-related Disclosures
standards.bodyFull: International Sustainability Standards Board, housed in the IFRS Foundation
standards.edition: Issued June 2023, effective from 1 January 2024. Amended by Amendments to Greenhouse Gas Emissions Disclosures (December 2025), effective from 1 January 2027 with early application permitted
standards.what: The global climate disclosure standard. It FULLY INCORPORATES the TCFD recommendations - governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets - and adds industry-based requirements derived from the SASB Standards, which is why the Financial Stability Board could call the ISSB standards the culmination of the TCFD's work and hand monitoring to the IFRS Foundation in July 2023. It requires disclosure of gross Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions measured per the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard unless a jurisdiction requires otherwise, the use of climate-related scenario analysis to assess strategic resilience, transition plan disclosure, and the amount of assets or business activities vulnerable to climate risk. The December 2025 amendments ease four specific pressure points: Scope 3 Category 15 may be limited to financed emissions as defined in IFRS S2, alternative classification systems may replace GICS for disaggregation, the jurisdictional relief to use a non-GHG-Protocol method is clarified, and jurisdiction-required Global Warming Potential values may be used even where they are not from the latest IPCC report. More than 30 jurisdictions representing over 55 percent of global GDP have announced steps to implement or align.
standards.why: It is the instrument that turned climate disclosure from a voluntary corporate gesture into something a securities regulator can require, and it did so by absorbing the framework the market had already adopted rather than replacing it.
standards.gameEffect: The disclosure standard that makes climate risk financially visible, and the mechanic that connects the physical map to the money. Adopting IFRS S2 forces the player to run scenario analysis against the game's own warming pathways and publish which of the city's assets sit in the flood, heat or wildfire exposure zones. Doing so raises borrowing costs on genuinely exposed assets immediately, which hurts, and unlocks adaptation finance and lower rates on assets the player has already hardened, which pays back. It is the loop that makes early adaptation spending rational rather than charitable.
standards.supersedes: TCFD Recommendations (2017), as the live monitored framework

standards.title: Recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
standards.bodyFull: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, created by the Financial Stability Board in December 2015 at the request of G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors
standards.edition: Final Recommendations, June 2017. The Task Force was disbanded in 2023
standards.what: The framework that invented the shape of climate disclosure: four pillars - governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets - which are now the single most reused piece of architecture in the field. In July 2023 the Financial Stability Board declared the Task Force's work complete and asked the IFRS Foundation to take over monitoring of companies' progress from 2024, calling the ISSB standards the culmination of the TCFD's work. The recommendations are not withdrawn and are not wrong; they are fully incorporated into IFRS S2. But the TCFD is not a live body, and a 2026 disclosure described as TCFD-aligned is describing a framework whose monitoring now belongs to the ISSB. The FSB still publishes annual progress reports on jurisdictional adoption; the November 2024 edition found most FSB jurisdictions have set or proposed requirements based on the ISSB standards and the TCFD recommendations.
standards.why: It is the clean example of a voluntary framework succeeding so completely that it was absorbed into mandatory standards and dissolved itself. Knowing that the four pillars survived while the body did not is the useful fact.
standards.gameEffect: The early-game disclosure option, available before IFRS S2 unlocks. Adopting the four pillars is cheap and gets the player a partial disclosure score and access to the voluntary investor networks. It becomes a legacy state once IFRS S2 is available: an organisation still reporting TCFD-only after the ISSB transition is flagged as behind and loses the score it was earning, which models the real transition pressure. The four pillars themselves are never wasted, because everything the player built for TCFD carries straight into IFRS S2.

standards.title: European Sustainability Reporting Standard E1: Climate change (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772)
standards.bodyFull: European Commission, standards drafted by EFRAG, adopted as a Delegated Regulation supplementing Directive 2013/34/EU
standards.edition: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 of 31 July 2023, Annex I published in the Official Journal 2023-12-22 (corrigendum 2024-04-18). Revised ESRS delegated act adopted 2026-07-03, to be used from financial year 2027
standards.what: The EU's mandatory climate reporting standard, one of the twelve in ESRS Set 1 and the one with teeth. E1 has nine disclosure requirements, E1-1 through E1-9: transition plan for climate change mitigation; policies; actions and resources; targets; energy consumption and mix; gross Scope 1, 2, 3 and total greenhouse gas emissions; GHG removals and carbon credits; internal carbon pricing; and the anticipated financial effects of material physical and transition risks. It applies through a materiality gate, and the gate is the EU's distinctive move: DOUBLE MATERIALITY requires the undertaking to consider both how climate affects the business (financial materiality, all IFRS S2 asks) and how the business affects climate and people (impact materiality). If climate is found not material, the undertaking must disclose that conclusion and its reasoning, which makes the gate hard to walk through quietly. A major simplification is in flight: Stop the Clock (Directive (EU) 2025/794), the quick-fix Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1416, and Omnibus I (Directive (EU) 2026/470, published 2026-02-26) led to a revised ESRS adopted 2026-07-03 that is roughly half the length with about 61 percent fewer mandatory datapoints and all voluntary disclosures deleted. The Omnibus value-chain cap does not cover the E1-8 gross Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions metrics.
standards.why: Double materiality is the deepest philosophical split in climate disclosure. IFRS S2 asks what climate does to your balance sheet; ESRS E1 also asks what your balance sheet does to the climate. The two answers are different and the difference is the whole argument about what disclosure is for.
standards.gameEffect: The European map's disclosure regime, and it is mandatory rather than chosen. Double materiality doubles the assessment work and surfaces impacts a purely financial assessment would miss, so the player sees emissions and harms their own operations cause even where those cost the city nothing directly. That visibility feeds a public-pressure meter that a financial-materiality-only regime never triggers. E1-9 anticipated financial effects forces the player to publish the projected cost of the climate risk on their own map, which raises borrowing costs on exposed districts and makes adaptation spending pay for itself. The 2026 simplification arrives as a mid-game event that cuts the reporting burden without touching the emissions metrics.

standards.title: CDP Cities, States and Regions disclosure (the CDP-ICLEI Track questionnaire)
standards.bodyFull: CDP (formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project), run in partnership with ICLEI - Local Governments for Sustainability
standards.edition: 2025 CDP-ICLEI Track and States & Regions Questionnaire and Guidance, April 2025; annual cycle
standards.what: A disclosure PLATFORM and a SCORING system, not a standard: it does not tell a city how to calculate its inventory, the GPC does that, it asks for the answer and grades the response. Its real value is that one submission satisfies many initiatives at once - ICLEI, C40, the Global Covenant of Mayors Common Reporting Framework, the WWF One Planet City Challenge, NetZeroCities Mission Cities, the Union of Baltic Cities Sustainable Cities Commission, RegionsAdapt and the Under2 Coalition - and it is aligned with Race to Resilience, Race to Zero, the EU Mission on Adaptation, the Science Based Targets Network and the TCFD. Before it, a city in five networks filled in five forms. The 2025 Cities questionnaire is split into three Pathways by jurisdiction attributes, with higher pathways carrying more questions, and only Pathway 1 disclosers were scored in 2025. Modules cover governance, climate risk and vulnerability, emissions inventory, sectoral data, adaptation goals, mitigation targets, planning, actions and forests. In the 2025 cycle the scoring deadline was 2025-09-17, the platform closed 2025-11-19, scores reached disclosers 2025-12-10, and only A-scoring jurisdictions were published in January 2026.
standards.why: It is the mechanism by which the voluntary city-climate world became comparable. A city's CDP score is the closest thing there is to a public grade on whether its climate plan is real.
standards.gameEffect: The annual report card, and the single best framing device for a city builder's scoring loop. Once a year the player submits: an inventory (from the GPC), a risk and vulnerability assessment, targets, adaptation goals and actions. The score comes back on the A to D scale and drives everything downstream - network membership, access to climate finance, investor confidence, and citizen trust. One submission covering eight networks is modelled directly as an administrative-cost saving over reporting to each separately. Pathway selection is a real choice: the higher pathway is more work but is the only one scored, so a city that stays on an easy pathway is invisible on the leaderboard however well it is actually doing.

standards.title: Adaptation to climate change - Principles, requirements and guidelines
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2019-06
standards.what: The umbrella adaptation standard. It puts an organisation through an adaptation cycle and uses 'shall' language in clauses 5 to 10, so it has real requirements: pre-planning (know your context before you plan), assessing impacts and uncertainties, adaptation planning, implementation, then monitoring, evaluation, reporting and communication. Clause 4 sets the principles the rest hangs on, including transparency, accountability, subsidiarity and not letting adaptation and mitigation work against each other. It is written to apply to anything from a business unit to a whole industrial sector, and other standards are built on top of it rather than beside it. Confirmed unchanged at ISO's 2024 systematic review, so it is the current edition.
standards.why: It is the standard that says adaptation is a management cycle you repeat, not a report you commission once. Everything else in the ISO adaptation family - 14091, 14092, 14093 - is written to fit inside its frame.
standards.gameEffect: Unlocks the adaptation cycle itself. Until the city adopts ISO 14090 it can only build defences reactively after a hazard has already hit a district; once adopted, the player gets a standing planning loop with a monitoring readout, and every later adaptation standard becomes buildable. Adaptation works done outside the cycle decay in effectiveness because nothing is monitoring them.

standards.title: Adaptation to climate change - Guidelines on vulnerability, impacts and risk assessment
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2021-02
standards.what: How to actually do a climate risk assessment. It uses the IPCC's decomposition of risk into hazard, exposure and vulnerability, where vulnerability is itself sensitivity plus adaptive capacity, and it asks you to build impact chains that trace a climate signal through to a consequence you care about. It covers setting the context, the objectives, the boundary and the time horizon, and it explicitly handles both present and future risk. Its annexes carry the working material: worked impact chains, screening matrices, sample indicators, aggregation methods. It is a guidance standard, not a certifiable one, and it deliberately excludes transition risk - it is about the physics arriving at your door, not the market repricing your assets.
standards.why: A city that has not done this does not know which of its districts will flood, bake or dry out first, and so cannot rank what to spend money on. This is the document that turns 'climate change is a risk' into a ranked list of places and assets.
standards.gameEffect: A district assessed to ISO 14091 shows its hazard overlay BEFORE you commit the build, not after the first flood. The tile reveals hazard, exposure and vulnerability as three separate bars, so the player can see that a low-hazard tile with a hospital and no backup power is still high risk. Unassessed districts build blind and their hazard is only revealed by an event.

standards.title: Climate change adaptation - Requirements and guidance on adaptation planning for local governments and communities
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition as a full International Standard, 2026-02-09, 43 pages, ISO/TC 207/SC 7
standards.what: The city-scale member of the adaptation family, and brand new in this form. It requires a local government to stand up an adaptation governance structure with a named facilitation team, run a vulnerability, impacts and risk assessment, set priorities with the people who will live with them, write an adaptation plan matched to local conditions, then monitor delivery and update the plan. It was published on 2026-02-09 as a full International Standard replacing ISO/TS 14092:2020, which is now withdrawn; the changes are updated guidance plus a new Annex D on actually implementing the measures rather than only planning them. It does not mandate any particular adaptation outcome - it mandates that you have a process and can show it.
standards.why: Adaptation finance increasingly asks a city to show an evidence-based, transparently governed plan before it releases money, and this is the international definition of one. It is also the only ISO adaptation standard written for a mayor rather than a company.
standards.gameEffect: Adopting it gives the city a permanent Adaptation Plan panel: hazards ranked, districts prioritised, and a review timer. Districts inside the plan get their protective works costed and sequenced automatically instead of being placed ad hoc, and the city becomes eligible for the adaptation-finance mechanism (see ISO 14093). Let the plan go unreviewed past its cycle and the priority ranking goes stale, silently mis-sorting your spending.

standards.title: Mechanism for financing local adaptation to climate change - Performance-based climate resilience grants - Requirements and guidelines
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2022-11
standards.what: A standard for the plumbing of adaptation money. It defines a country-based mechanism that channels climate finance down to subnational authorities through performance-based climate resilience grants: the local government gets a top-up on its normal fiscal transfer, spends it on resilience, and the next grant depends on verified performance. It sets requirements for programming the expenditure, verifying it was climate expenditure, and auditing the result. It was built from the UN Capital Development Fund's LoCAL Facility, which had been running or being designed in 34 countries when the standard launched at COP27 in 2022.
standards.why: Adaptation fails most often at the money, not the engineering. This is the only ISO standard that describes how the cash reaches the district that needs the drain, and it makes the next tranche conditional on the last one having worked.
standards.gameEffect: Turns adaptation funding from a flat annual grant into a performance loop. Verified resilience spending in one cycle raises the next cycle's grant; unverified or misclassified spending cuts it. The player learns the real lesson fast, which is that you have to be able to PROVE the culvert was built and that it was a climate measure, not merely to have built it.

standards.title: Sustainable cities and communities - Indicators for resilient cities
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2019-12, ISO/TC 268; confirmed at systematic review 2025
standards.what: The closest thing in the world to a written specification for a resilient city. It defines around 68 indicators across nineteen ISO city themes, each with a stated method so two cities' numbers can be compared: economy (historical and average annual disaster loss as a share of city product, share of properties insured against high-risk hazards), energy (number of electricity sources each supplying at least 5 percent of capacity, supply capacity as a percentage of peak demand, share of critical facilities on off-grid energy), environment and climate change (magnitude of the urban heat island, annual frequency of extreme rainfall, heat, cold and flood events, tree canopy as a share of city land area, share of city surface in high-albedo materials), governance (how often disaster-management plans are updated, share of essential services with a documented continuity plan, share of city data with secure remote backup), housing (share of buildings structurally vulnerable to high-risk hazards, share of residential properties in high-risk zones, share of damaged infrastructure 'built back better'), safety (share of population covered by a multi-hazard early warning system), urban planning (share of city area covered by publicly available hazard maps, pervious and porous surface as a share of land area, annual number of critical infrastructures flooded), water (number of sources each supplying at least 5 percent of water capacity, share of population supplyable with drinking water by alternative means for 72 hours), food (share of population servable by city food reserves for 72 hours), and transport (evacuation routes per 100,000 people). Deliberately, it sets NO target values - it standardises the measurement, not the pass mark, and a city may only claim conformity with the measurement. It is designed to be implemented alongside ISO 37120 and inside an ISO 37101 management system, and its annexes map every indicator onto the risk-management process, the disaster-management process, the SDGs and the Sendai Framework.
standards.why: It is the answer to 'what does resilient actually mean, numerically'. Two of its indicators, the 72-hour water and food rules and the 5-percent source-diversity rules, are effectively design targets a city can build to.
standards.gameEffect: This is the game's scoreboard. Every ISO 37123 indicator the city can measure becomes a live readout, and several become direct win conditions: at least two electricity sources and two water sources each carrying 5 percent or more of capacity, 72 hours of alternative drinking water and food reserves for the population, an evacuation-route count per 100,000, hazard maps published over the city area. Because the standard sets no thresholds, the game supplies them and says so on the tooltip - that honesty is itself the teaching moment.

standards.title: Sustainable cities and communities - Indicators for city services and quality of life
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: Second edition, 2018-07, 121 pages; stage 90.92, International Standard to be revised; a third edition (ISO/AWI 37120) was registered 2025-11-18
standards.what: The base layer of the ISO city indicator family: 104 indicators across nineteen themes covering city services and quality of life, each with a defined method so that a number from one city means the same as a number from another. Each theme carries one core indicator that any implementer should report, a profile indicator, and a set of supporting indicators. It replaced ISO 37120:2014, dropping fire and emergency response and shelter and adding housing, population and social conditions, sport and culture, and urban agriculture. ISO 37123 and ISO 37122 are both written to be reported ON TOP of it, not instead of it. A third edition is in preparation, so cite the 2018 edition but expect it to move.
standards.why: Resilience is measured as the ability to keep delivering ordinary city services under stress, so you need the ordinary-service numbers first. Without ISO 37120 the resilience indicators have no baseline to be a departure from.
standards.gameEffect: The city's baseline service dashboard, and the denominator for every resilience score. A district's resilience rating is computed as service delivery under stress divided by ISO 37120 normal-conditions service delivery, so a city that never measured its normal state cannot score its disrupted one.

standards.title: Sustainable cities and communities - Indicators for smart cities
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2019-05, 95 pages; confirmed at systematic review 2024-10-28
standards.what: The instrumentation layer. Same nineteen themes and same house method as ISO 37120, but the indicators measure how much of the city is actually sensed, connected and digitally managed: real-time monitoring coverage, smart metering penetration, open data, digital service delivery. It is explicitly meant to be reported alongside ISO 37120 rather than on its own, and ISO records it as contributing to both mitigation and adaptation.
standards.why: You cannot run a heat-health warning or a flood alert for a district you are not measuring. The smart-city indicators are, in practice, the measurement precondition for most of the resilience indicators.
standards.gameEffect: Sensor and metering coverage from ISO 37122 sets the RESOLUTION of every hazard readout. An uninstrumented district reports its flood depth or heat index as a coarse city-wide average; a fully metered one reports per-tile and in real time, which is the difference between evacuating a street and evacuating a borough.

standards.title: Sustainable cities and communities - Guidance on the use of ISO 37120, ISO 37122 and ISO 37123
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2024-04, 32 pages, ISO/TC 268
standards.what: The manual for the other three. Across ISO 37120, 37122 and 37123 there are 292 indicators, which is more than any city can start with, so this document tells a local government how to sequence adoption, where the data comes from, how to handle a theme it cannot yet measure, and how to keep the three sets consistent with each other. It is guidance, with no indicators of its own.
standards.why: The indicator family's real failure mode is a city that buys all three standards and reports none of them. This is the document that makes the family usable by a normal municipal team.
standards.gameEffect: A tutorial and sequencing unlock rather than an effect. Adopting it turns the 292-indicator wall into a staged checklist, so the player is shown the ten indicators worth measuring first for the hazards their map actually has.

standards.title: Sustainable development in communities - Management system for sustainable development - Requirements with guidance for use
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2016-07, 32 pages, plus Amendment 1:2024 (2024-02-23); confirmed at systematic review 2025
standards.what: A management system standard, in the same family as ISO 14001, but for a community rather than a company. Its mechanism is a cross-analysis: every strategy, programme, project, plan and service the community runs must be evaluated for its contribution to six purposes of sustainability - resilience is one of them, alongside attractiveness, preservation of the environment, responsible resource use, social cohesion and well-being - while taking twelve sustainability issues into account. Tables 2 to 13 supply the questions to ask in that cross-analysis. Conformity is all-or-nothing: you cannot claim ISO 37101 with exclusions. ISO 37123 names it as a normative reference and follows its principles.
standards.why: It is what stops resilience from being a separate department. Under ISO 37101 a transport scheme and a housing scheme both have to answer for their contribution to resilience, in the same review, on the same form.
standards.gameEffect: Mainstreaming. Once the city runs an ISO 37101 management system, EVERY building - not just the flood wall and the cooling centre - is scored against the six purposes at placement, and the player sees a resilience delta on an ordinary road or school. Without it, only things tagged as resilience infrastructure count, which is exactly the mistake the standard exists to prevent.

standards.title: Risk management - Guidelines
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: Second edition, 2018-02
standards.what: The generic risk grammar everything else borrows. It gives eight principles, a governance framework led from the top, and a process: communication and consultation, establishing the scope and context, risk assessment (identification, analysis, evaluation), risk treatment, monitoring and review, then recording and reporting. The 2018 revision pushed leadership and integration into governance to the front, stressed that the process is iterative rather than annual, and moved most of the vocabulary out into ISO Guide 73. It explicitly cannot be certified against, which is why serious users say 'aligned to ISO 31000' rather than 'certified'.
standards.why: ISO 14091's climate risk assessment is a specialisation of this process, and ISO 37123 maps its resilience indicators onto it in Annex B. Learn this shape once and the rest of the family reads easily.
standards.gameEffect: The risk register. Adopting ISO 31000 gives the city a persistent list of identified risks with analysis, evaluation and a treatment decision on each, and treatment options become visible as buildable actions (avoid, reduce, transfer to insurance, retain). Risks the player never entered on the register still fire as events but arrive with no pre-costed treatment, so the response is improvised and more expensive.

standards.title: Security and resilience - Business continuity management systems - Requirements
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: Second edition, 2019-10
standards.what: The one certifiable standard in this set, and the one with hard numbers in it. It requires a documented business continuity management system built on a business impact analysis that, for every critical activity, sets a maximum tolerable period of disruption, a recovery time objective and a recovery point objective, and traces each to evidence rather than to a comfortable guess. Clause 8 requires recovery strategies, written continuity plans and an exercising and testing programme against scenarios realistic for the organisation's risk profile, with the gaps found in testing fed back into the plans. It follows ISO's Annex SL structure so it bolts onto other management systems. Guidance on using it is in ISO 22313:2020.
standards.why: ISO 37123 asks what share of a city's essential services and essential service providers have a documented continuity plan. This is the standard that defines what counts as one, and its RTO is the number that decides whether a hospital is dark for two hours or two days.
standards.gameEffect: Every essential service building gets an RTO in hours, set by whether it holds an ISO 22301-conformant plan and whether that plan has been exercised. When an event knocks out a district, certified services come back inside their RTO and uncertified ones roll a much longer outage. Exercises cost money and time and must be repeated - a plan written once and never tested degrades to an uncertified outage.

standards.title: Security and resilience - Emergency management - Guidelines for incident management
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: Second edition, 2018-11; reviewed and confirmed 2024
standards.what: How multiple organisations run one incident without tripping over each other. It sets out incident-management principles, the basic components - process and structure, roles and responsibilities, tasks, resource management - and, crucially, joint direction and cooperation for the case where two or more organisations respond together, either keeping their own command structures or merging into a combined one. Command and control and information management are the two spines: who decides, and how accurate information is collected, analysed and pushed out. It is a guidelines standard, so despite what some vendors sell, it is not an accredited certification scheme.
standards.why: Urban disasters are always multi-agency. The failure mode is not that nobody responded, it is that fire, water, power and the mayor's office each ran a separate incident with a different picture of the map.
standards.gameEffect: Sets the coordination penalty during an event. With ISO 22320 adopted, all responding agencies share one incident map and one command chain, and response effectiveness stays flat as more agencies join. Without it, each additional responding agency adds a coordination penalty, so a big multi-hazard event gets WORSE the more help arrives - which is the real-world behaviour the standard exists to stop.

standards.title: Security and resilience - Community resilience - Principles, framework and guidelines on urban resilience
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2024-12, ISO/TC 292
standards.what: The full standard for urban resilience, and the successor to the 2020 technical report ISO/TR 22370. It defines urban resilience as the ability of an urban system, with its inhabitants, in a changing environment, to anticipate, prepare for, respond to and absorb shocks, positively adapt and transform under stress and uncertainty, while still delivering inclusive and sustainable development. It splits urban resilience into three domains - people and communities, governance and public services, and trade and business services - and gives guidance on how to organise, assess, plan, implement and continually improve it, with explicit attention to the most disadvantaged and vulnerable residents. It applies to all urban contexts and all governance structures, at every level of risk.
standards.why: It is the document that puts the word 'resilience' on a definition a city can be held to, and it insists that a city which protects its averages while abandoning its most vulnerable neighbourhoods has not become resilient.
standards.gameEffect: Splits the city's single resilience score into the standard's three domains - people, governance and services, business - and adds an equity check: the score is dragged down by the WORST-served district, not lifted by the average. A city that hardens its downtown and leaves an informal settlement exposed scores badly, which is exactly the lesson.

standards.title: Security and resilience - Community resilience - Guidelines for infrastructure resilience
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2025-11, 33 pages, ISO/TC 292
standards.what: Guidelines for establishing, maintaining, monitoring and improving infrastructure resilience so that essential services keep running. It is built directly on UNDRR's Principles for Resilient Infrastructure and was developed with UNDRR's contribution. Its distinguishing move is that it works across sectors and across borders, treating infrastructure as a system of systems rather than a list of assets, and it is aimed at informing policy, strategy and regulatory frameworks from evidence about risk and vulnerability. Annex A gives an example governance framework. It deliberately does NOT cover emergency management and response - that is ISO 22320's job.
standards.why: It is the standard that formalises the thing every operator knows and no asset register records: the water treatment plant needs the substation, the substation needs the road, and the road needs the pumps that keep the underpass dry. UNDRR calls the annual direct disaster loss it is aimed at more than 300 billion US dollars.
standards.gameEffect: Turns the utility networks into a dependency graph the player can see. Placing a water plant draws its power, road and telecoms dependencies as live links; cutting any one of them takes the plant down even though the plant itself is undamaged. Building to ISO 22372 lets the player add redundancy on the DEPENDENCY rather than the asset, which is usually far cheaper, and it is the only route to the ISO 37123 source-diversity indicators.

standards.title: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030
standards.bodyFull: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
standards.edition: Adopted 2015-03-18 at the Third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction, Sendai, Japan; 15-year term to 2030
standards.what: A voluntary, non-binding intergovernmental agreement that replaced the Hyogo Framework for Action and put the primary duty to reduce disaster risk on the State. It has four priorities for action - understanding disaster risk, strengthening disaster risk governance, investing in disaster risk reduction for resilience, and enhancing preparedness for response and to build back better in recovery - and seven global targets, each measured. Target A: substantially reduce global disaster mortality per 100,000 in 2020-2030 against 2005-2015. Target B: the same for the number of people affected. Target C: reduce direct disaster economic loss as a share of global GDP. Target D: substantially reduce damage to critical infrastructure and disruption of basic services including health and education facilities. Target E: substantially increase the number of countries with national and local disaster risk reduction strategies, by 2020. Target F: enhance international cooperation to developing countries. Target G: substantially increase availability of and access to multi-hazard early warning systems and disaster risk information, by 2030. Progress is tracked through 38 indicators reported to the Sendai Framework Monitor.
standards.why: It is the global scoreboard every city resilience instrument reports into - ISO 37123 maps its indicators to it in Annex D, and UNDRR's city Scorecard is built to answer it. Targets D and G are the two a city can move directly.
standards.gameEffect: The campaign's global objective layer. The city contributes to the seven targets and sees its share: mortality per 100,000, people affected, economic loss as a share of city product, critical-infrastructure damage, whether it has a local DRR strategy at all (Target E is a yes/no the player can just DO), and the fraction of population covered by multi-hazard early warning (Target G). Targets are measured as a decadal average, so a single good year does not move them - the player has to hold the line.

standards.title: Principles for Resilient Infrastructure
standards.bodyFull: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
standards.edition: First edition, 2022-05, following consultations with representatives of over 100 countries hosted with the Government of Qatar
standards.what: Six principles and 33 key actions for national infrastructure systems: continuously learning, proactively protected, environmentally integrated, socially engaged, shared responsibility, and adaptively transforming. Proactively protected means hazards are designed for up front, and it explicitly covers pandemics, terrorism and cyber-attack as well as natural hazards. Environmentally integrated means nature-based solutions and ecosystem data inside the decision, not bolted on afterwards. The principles are pitched at national-scale net resilience gain rather than at scoring an individual asset, and they are the foundation ISO 22372:2025 was built on.
standards.why: Free, short, and the direct ancestor of the paywalled ISO standard - which makes it the honest entry point for anyone who cannot buy ISO 22372. It also supports Sendai Target D on critical infrastructure damage.
standards.gameEffect: A set of six modifiers rather than a building. Each principle the city adopts changes how infrastructure is placed: proactively protected raises build cost but sets the asset's hazard rating at design time; environmentally integrated makes nature-based options (wetland, floodplain, urban forest) count as infrastructure with a maintenance line; continuously learning means every event the city survives permanently improves the design standard of everything built afterwards.

standards.code: UNDRR Disaster Resilience Scorecard for Cities
standards.title: Disaster Resilience Scorecard for Cities (Preliminary and Detailed levels), with thematic addenda
standards.bodyFull: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (Making Cities Resilient 2030)
standards.edition: Detailed level, May 2017; maintained and extended under MCR2030 with addenda for extreme heat, multi-hazard early warning, education, food systems and cultural heritage
standards.what: A self-assessment instrument, not a standard - and worth naming as such. It scores a city against UNDRR's Ten Essentials for Making Cities Resilient, covering governance, risk assessment, financial planning, urban development, infrastructure resilience, ecosystems, social inclusion, preparedness and recovery planning. Two levels: the Preliminary level has 47 criteria scored 0 to 3 and is designed for a one to two day multi-stakeholder workshop; the Detailed level has 117 criteria scored 0 to 5. Scores are weighted per essential because the essentials have different numbers of indicators. It asks a city to name a most-probable and a most-severe scenario per hazard, and pairs with the Quick Risk Estimation tool where there is no capacity for full analysis. The extreme-heat addendum is one of the few structured heat-resilience assessment instruments in existence.
standards.why: It is free, it is a workshop rather than a purchase, and it is how most cities in the world actually start. It is also the practical baseline for a local DRR strategy under Sendai Target E.
standards.gameEffect: The city audit. Running the Scorecard costs time and staff but reveals the city's weakest essentials as a ranked list of gaps, converting fog into a to-do list. The Preliminary level is cheap and coarse; the Detailed level costs far more and exposes gaps the preliminary one misses entirely. The extreme-heat addendum unlocks the heat mechanics.

standards.title: Cities Climate Transition Framework
