standards.bodyFull: C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group
standards.edition: Published 2023-12, updating the Climate Action Planning Framework (2018)
standards.what: Not a standard but a membership requirement, which in practice makes it binding on the cities it covers. It sets five essential components a city climate action plan must have: emissions neutrality, building resilience, inclusivity and benefits, governance and mainstreaming, and monitoring progress. Every C40 member city's plan is reviewed by a cross-disciplinary expert group for alignment with it, and developing and implementing a Paris-aligned plan under this framework is a condition of remaining a member. It replaced the 2018 Climate Action Planning Framework - which had been built with Boston, Durban, London, Los Angeles, Melbourne, Mexico City, New York and Paris - to reflect five years of delivery experience and the recommendations of the UN High-Level Expert Group's Integrity Matters report.
standards.why: It is the clearest statement anywhere that a city climate plan which cuts emissions but does not build resilience is an incomplete plan. It also carries a real enforcement mechanism, which almost nothing else in this lane does.
standards.gameEffect: A membership contract with teeth. Joining C40 gives the city access to peer knowledge and finance channels, but the plan is audited on a cycle against all five components: neglect resilience or equity while chasing emissions and the audit fails, and the benefits lapse. It is the game's main counter to the player who optimises a single number.

standards.title: Global Covenant of Mayors Common Reporting Framework, Version 7.0
standards.bodyFull: Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy
standards.edition: Version 7.0, April 2023 (final file dated 2023-09-14); supersedes Version 6.1 (2018)
standards.what: The single reporting specification that all GCoM regional covenants share, so that a city in Lagos and a city in Lisbon report comparable numbers. Three pillars: mitigation, adaptation, and - added in v7.0 and launched at COP27 - energy access and poverty, structured on secure, affordable and sustainable energy with more than 50 indicators. On the adaptation side it sets requirements for a climate risk and vulnerability assessment: the city identifies its most significant hazards and reports, for each, a current risk level as probability times consequence, plus the adaptive capacity of both the local government and the community. Progress is recognised with badges awarded per pillar as the city moves from commitment to assessment to target to plan to monitoring. v7.0 also added a simplified reporting level for local governments with low data capacity.
standards.why: GCoM has more than 12,500 signatory cities, which makes the CRF the largest single dataset of city climate action in the world. Its risk-and-vulnerability requirement is many cities' first formal climate risk assessment.
standards.gameEffect: The reporting minigame and the diplomacy layer. The city earns badges by completing the sequence assessment, target, plan, monitoring for each of the three pillars, and badges unlock finance and partner offers. The simplified reporting level is available to a low-capacity city at reduced benefit - a deliberate teaching point that the framework meets a city where it is rather than excluding it.

standards.title: Statutory flood protection standards for primary flood defences (Waterwet Annexes II and III, 2017; base protection level now in the Environment and Planning Act, Omgevingswet Art. 2.15(2))
standards.bodyFull: Government of the Netherlands, via the Delta Programme and the Delta Decision on Flood Risk Management
standards.edition: In force 2017-01-01; the Water Act (2009) was absorbed into the Environment and Planning Act in January 2024, which now carries the base protection level
standards.what: The most stringent flood protection law in the world, and the first national standard anywhere set on a quantitative estimate of flood PROBABILITY including levee failure rather than on water-level exceedance. Two things are set. First, a base protection level: by 2050 at the latest, the probability of dying as a result of a flood must not exceed 1 in 100,000 per year for everyone living behind a primary defence - a personal fatality risk, not a dike failure rate. Second, a failure probability standard for each of more than 200 individual dike segments, ranging from 1 in 300 to 1 in 1,000,000 per year, set from the cost of strengthening that segment against the consequences of it failing, so segments protecting dense population, high economic value or nationally vital infrastructure get far stricter numbers. This replaced the old ring-levee exceedance standards of 1 in 1,250 to 1 in 10,000. Delivery runs through the Flood Protection Programme (HWBP), covering roughly 2,000 km of dikes and over 400 structures; about 80 percent of the roughly 9 million people behind a primary defence already had the base level in 2020.
standards.why: It is the working proof that a country can set a flood standard as a risk number per person rather than a design storm, and then legislate segment-by-segment budgets against it. Every other national flood regime looks under-specified next to it.
standards.gameEffect: The hardest and most expensive flood standard the player can adopt, and the only one that prices protection by CONSEQUENCE. Each defence segment gets its own required failure probability, computed from the population, economic value and critical infrastructure behind it, so protecting an empty polder is cheap and protecting a dense district with a hospital is enormously dear. The city-wide win condition is individual fatality risk at or below 1 in 100,000 per year everywhere behind a defence - and 'everywhere' is the hard part, because one weak segment fails the whole city.

standards.title: Flood plain management criteria for flood-prone areas, National Flood Insurance Program
standards.bodyFull: Federal Emergency Management Agency, United States
standards.edition: Codified at 44 CFR Part 60 Subpart A, amended continuously; current text on eCFR
standards.what: The US floor, and it is a low one. A community that wants its residents to be able to buy federal flood insurance must adopt floodplain management regulations at least as strict as 44 CFR 60.3. The core requirement is that in a Special Flood Hazard Area - the 1 percent annual chance, or 100-year, floodplain - the lowest floor of a new or substantially improved residential building must be at or above the Base Flood Elevation. Freeboard, meaning any margin ABOVE the BFE, is NOT required by the NFIP; FEMA encourages at least one foot, and many communities voluntarily adopt one to three feet. The BFE is a regulatory line drawn from historical hydrology on a Flood Insurance Rate Map, so by construction it does not include future sea level rise or changed rainfall.
standards.why: Most American floodplain building is built to exactly this and no more, which means it is built to a historical 1-in-100 with zero margin. Understanding that the NFIP minimum is a minimum, and a backward-looking one, explains most US urban flood damage.
standards.gameEffect: The default, cheapest flood rule and the one the game should let the player regret. Building to the NFIP minimum lets buildings sit exactly at BFE with no margin: they survive the modelled 100-year flood and are destroyed by anything above it, and because the game's BFE is drawn from the historical record, a warming scenario makes those buildings fail more and more often without the map ever changing. Adopting local freeboard of 1 to 3 feet is a cheap upgrade the player can choose - and the numbers should show it paying for itself.

standards.title: Flood Resistant Design and Construction
standards.bodyFull: American Society of Civil Engineers / Structural Engineering Institute
standards.edition: ASCE/SEI 24-24, published 2025, replacing ASCE 24-14; submitted for reference in the 2027 IBC
standards.what: The US engineering standard for building in a flood hazard area, written to meet or exceed NFIP minimums, and the 2024 edition changes its basis fundamentally. It extends the flood hazard area to include the 500-year floodplain (Shaded X Zone) as well as the 100-year SFHA. And instead of the old approach of BFE plus a freeboard from a table, the Design Flood Elevation is now the greater of the community's own elevation or the elevation of a mean recurrence interval flood set by the building's Flood Design Class, plus sea level rise: Flood Design Class 2, most commercial and residential buildings, elevates to the 500-year flood; Class 3 to the 750-year; Class 4, the essential facilities, to the 1,000-year. Flood loads come from ASCE 7-22 Supplement 2. It also sets maximum deployment times for active dry floodproofing by Flood Design Class, and adds requirements on flood mitigation pumps and valves, utility placement, inspection and maintenance, and flood emergency operation plans. ASCE 24-14 is what is currently referenced by the International Building Code.
standards.why: This is the moment US flood engineering stopped designing to a historical 100-year line and started designing to a recurrence interval chosen by how much the building matters. It is the technical answer to everything wrong with the NFIP minimum.
standards.gameEffect: The player assigns each building a Flood Design Class and the game elevates it to the matching recurrence interval - 500, 750 or 1,000 year - plus projected sea level rise, with cost scaling accordingly. A hospital placed as Class 4 is expensive and survives events that erase the Class 2 housing around it. Dry floodproofing is available but carries a deployment time: if the warning lead time from the early warning system is shorter than the deployment time, it simply does not deploy.

standards.title: Federal Flood Risk Management Standard
standards.bodyFull: United States federal government, implemented by FEMA (44 CFR Part 9) and HUD
standards.edition: Created by Executive Order 13690 (2015); revoked by EO 13807 (2017); reinstated by EO 14030 (2021); FEMA final rule effective 2024-09-09; FEMA implementation halted 2025-03-25; EO 14030 revoked 2025-01-20; HUD rescission proposed 2026-07-10
standards.what: A federal rule that required federally funded projects to be built above the 100-year floodplain, using one of three approaches: the Climate-Informed Science Approach, using best-available data on future flooding; the Freeboard Value Approach, adding 2 feet above BFE for non-critical actions and 3 feet for critical ones; or the 0.2 percent annual chance (500-year) elevation. It is included here BECAUSE it was withdrawn, and the sequence is the lesson: created 2015, revoked 2017, reinstated 2021, finalised as a FEMA rule effective 2024-09-09, then halted for FEMA-funded projects effective 2025-03-25, with FEMA reverting to the 1 percent floodplain for non-critical and 0.2 percent for critical actions. EO 14030, its legal basis, was revoked on 2025-01-20. HUD's parallel rule, which from 2025-01-01 required new FHA-insured construction in a Special Flood Hazard Area to be 2 feet above BFE, was still in force when a rescission was PROPOSED on 2026-07-10 with comments open to 2026-09-08. Verify before relying on either.
standards.why: It is the clearest available case of a resilience standard being switched on and off by politics rather than by evidence, four times in ten years. A game about building to standards should show that standards can be repealed.
standards.gameEffect: A national policy toggle outside the player's control. When the FFRMS is on, all publicly funded builds get 2 feet of freeboard free, or 3 for critical facilities; when it is repealed mid-campaign, everything built afterwards reverts to bare BFE while the older stock keeps its margin. Districts then show a visible split in flood survival by construction date, and the player has to decide whether to fund the margin locally out of city money.

standards.code: EA climate change allowances (flood risk assessments)
standards.title: Flood risk assessments: climate change allowances
standards.bodyFull: Environment Agency, England
standards.edition: Live GOV.UK guidance, revised repeatedly; current allowances derived from UKCP18
standards.what: England's mechanism for making a flood risk assessment face the future. An allowance is a percentage uplift applied to a baseline peak river flow or peak rainfall intensity to represent likely future conditions, published by river basin district and derived from the UK Climate Projections 2018. Because the projections are uncertain, the Environment Agency publishes bands rather than a single number - central (50th percentile), higher central (70th) and upper end (95th) - and the applicant picks the band from the development's vulnerability classification under NPPF Annex 3, its flood zone and its intended lifetime, which for housing is normally taken as 100 years. In practice, an EA consultation response typically asks for finished floor levels 300 mm above the 1 percent annual exceedance probability (1 in 100 year) level WITH the appropriate climate change allowance, and for any lost floodplain storage to be replaced. A worked strategic assessment might run surface water at 1 in 30 plus 35 percent and 1 in 100 plus 45 percent. The Environment Agency has said it is not resourced to re-run its own models with updated allowances, so the burden sits with the developer, and allowances get revised - one scheme saw a new allowance raise the predicted 1-in-100-plus-climate-change level by 300 mm.
standards.why: It is a rare, concrete, publicly documented method for putting a climate projection directly into a building's floor level, and the honest treatment of uncertainty - bands, not a number - is exactly the register this project cares about.
standards.gameEffect: The player chooses a percentile band when placing anything in a flood zone. Central is cheap and fails more often as the scenario warms; upper end costs more and holds. Because the allowance is revised on a timer during play, buildings designed to an old allowance quietly fall below standard - the tile does not change colour, but its flood survival does, which teaches the difference between compliant-when-built and safe-now.

standards.title: National Standards for Sustainable Drainage Systems
standards.bodyFull: Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, England
standards.edition: Published 2025-06-19, replacing the non-statutory technical standards of March 2015
standards.what: Seven standards for surface water drainage on major development in England (10 or more dwellings, 0.5 ha or more residential, 1 ha or more non-residential), and the first substantial update in a decade. Standard 1 is a hierarchy: it sets the order of preference for where runoff finally goes, putting rainwater harvesting and infiltration above discharge to a sewer. Standards 2 to 7 are fixed minimum design criteria: interception of the first 5 mm of rainfall on site, peak flow control to greenfield runoff rates using upper-end climate change allowances, a formal water quality risk assessment, amenity integration, a contribution to Biodiversity Net Gain, and a maintenance plan with named adoption responsibilities. The 2015 standards they replace covered essentially only peak flow rate and volume, with nothing on water quality, biodiversity, amenity or maintenance. The catch, and it is a large one: Schedule 3 of the Flood and Water Management Act 2010 remains uncommenced in England, so there is no statutory SuDS Approving Body and the standards are delivered through planning policy rather than law. Wales commenced Schedule 3 and SuDS are mandatory there.
standards.why: Two real lessons in one document. First, the numbers: 5 mm interception and greenfield-rate peak control are the concrete design targets that stop a new development making the flood downstream worse. Second, the gap: a good standard with no statutory approving body behind it is delivered unevenly, and England is the live experiment.
standards.gameEffect: Unlocks the SuDS drainage chain - permeable paving, swales, bioretention, detention basins, ponds, green and blue roofs, rainwater harvesting - and enforces the hierarchy, so the player cannot pipe straight to the sewer while an infiltration option exists. A district meeting the 5 mm interception and greenfield peak-rate rules stops exporting flood risk to downstream tiles, and its SuDS features simultaneously score on the ISO 37123 pervious-area indicator and on biodiversity. Skip the maintenance plan and the features silt up and stop working after some years, which is the real-world failure mode.
standards.supersedes: Sustainable drainage systems: non-statutory technical standards (Defra, 2015)

standards.title: The SuDS Manual
standards.bodyFull: Construction Industry Research and Information Association, UK
standards.edition: C753, published 2015-11-13, replacing C697 (2007); free to download
standards.what: The technical backbone under the UK SuDS standards, and it is free. It covers planning, design, construction and maintenance of sustainable drainage for both new and existing development, with component-level detail for rainwater harvesting, green roofs, infiltration systems, filter strips and filter drains, swales, bioretention, trees, pervious pavements, attenuation storage, detention basins, ponds and wetlands, plus how to calculate the hydraulic requirement and how to limit pollution. Its organising idea is the four pillars of SuDS design - water quantity, water quality, amenity and biodiversity - which is where the 2025 national standards got their broader scope from. It is best-practice guidance, not law, and local plan policies typically require adherence to it alongside Approved Document H of the Building Regulations.
standards.why: It is the document that turns 'put in a SuDS' into a buildable, maintainable, sized thing, and it is one of the very few openly readable technical references in this whole lane.
standards.gameEffect: The component catalogue behind the SuDS unlock. Each SuDS feature the player places carries C753's four pillars as four separate contributions - quantity, quality, amenity, biodiversity - so a detention basin and a wetland with the same storage volume score very differently on the last three, and the player learns that a drainage decision is also a park decision.

standards.title: Drinking water, wastewater and stormwater systems and services - Adaptation of water services to climate change impacts - Part 2: Stormwater services
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2024-06, ISO/TC 224
standards.what: The stormwater member of a four-part series that is, unusually, about climate change adaptation specifically rather than resilience in general. Part 1 (2023) sets the assessment principles for integrating climate change impacts into a water utility's planning and design; Part 2 (2024) applies them to stormwater services, including combined sewer systems for collection, transport, storage and treatment of stormwater; Part 3 (2025) covers drinking water services and Part 4 (2025) covers wastewater services, including non-combined systems. Part 2 asks a utility to identify and assess how climate change alters the loads on its stormwater system - rainfall intensity, event frequency, coincident sea level - and then to build adaptation strategies from that assessment rather than from the historical design storm.
standards.why: Almost every urban flood standard is about protecting buildings. This one is about the pipes, and it is the only international standard series that tells a water utility how to re-derive its design storm for a changed climate.
standards.gameEffect: Applies to the drainage NETWORK rather than to buildings. A stormwater system upgraded under ISO 24566-2 has its design storm re-derived on the scenario the player is running, so its capacity tracks the climate instead of the historical record; an un-adapted network keeps the design it was built with and starts surcharging as rainfall intensity rises, flooding streets that never flooded before while every individual building still passes its own flood standard.

standards.title: Activities relating to drinking water and wastewater services - Crisis management of water utilities
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: First edition, 2015-08, ISO/TC 224; reviewed and confirmed 2022
standards.what: Guidance for a water utility of any size, public or private, to build and run a crisis management system on a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle. It addresses the situation where normal potable supply, or wastewater collection and treatment, is interrupted, and it works through the phases: what to do before, listing the preparation steps for the pre-crisis phase; what to do during, covering quantity and quality of supply, sanitation, keeping the supply and sewage systems operating; and how to restore service and learn from it afterwards. It puts real weight on public communication, on the grounds that panic and lost trust are part of the damage. It is complemented by ISO/TS 24520 on the technical good practice, ISO 24527:2020 on alternative drinking water service provision during a crisis, and ISO 24595:2024 on alternative water service for essential facilities.
standards.why: A city that loses drinking water for three days has had a disaster regardless of what else survived. ISO 37123 asks what share of the population can be supplied with drinking water by alternative methods for 72 hours; this family is how that capability gets built.
standards.gameEffect: Gives the water utility a crisis mode. With ISO 24518 adopted, a water outage triggers a prepared response - alternative supply points, tankers, boil notices, public messaging - and the population served falls gradually; without it, the outage is total and public trust collapses, which raises the cost of every subsequent civic project. Pairs with the 72-hour alternative-supply indicator as the target the response has to hit.

standards.title: Risk and Resilience Management of Water and Wastewater Systems
standards.bodyFull: American Water Works Association (American National Standard, ANSI-designated)
standards.edition: AWWA J100-21, revising J100-10 (R13)
standards.what: The American National Standard for all-hazards risk and resilience analysis in the water sector, built on a seven-step process derived from RAMCAP Plus, developed by AWWA with the ASME Innovative Technologies Institute. It treats risk as a function of consequence, vulnerability and likelihood, and it covers three hazard families explicitly: malevolent acts, natural hazards, and - the part that matters most for a city builder - DEPENDENCY AND PROXIMITY hazards, meaning the utility fails because something it depends on failed, or because something dangerous was next door. Its stated purpose is to let owners allocate limited money well. It carries a DHS SAFETY Act designation. The related legal duty is separate: America's Water Infrastructure Act 2018 section 2013 amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to require every community water system serving more than 3,300 people to complete a risk and resilience assessment and an emergency response plan, certify both to EPA, and redo them every five years. EPA does not mandate J100 specifically - it recommends it alongside its own VSAT tool - so the ASSESSMENT is compulsory and the METHOD is not.
standards.why: It is the clearest published treatment of dependency and proximity hazard anywhere in this lane, and it is the standard behind a genuine legal mandate covering most of the US urban population.
standards.gameEffect: The water utility's version of the dependency graph. Running a J100 assessment on a plant reveals not only its direct hazards but its dependency hazards - the substation, the chemical supply chain, the access road - and its proximity hazards, such as a fuel depot next door. The five-year re-certification is a recurring cost the player must budget: let it lapse on a system serving more than 3,300 people and the city is out of compliance, with the penalty landing before any flood does.

standards.title: Heat-health action plans: guidance, second edition
standards.bodyFull: World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe, coordinated by the WHO European Centre for Environment, Climate Change and Health, Bonn
standards.edition: Second edition, launched 2026-06-11 in Berlin on Heat Action Day; first edition 2008
standards.what: The current international template for a city or national heat-health action plan, and far more implementation-oriented than the 2008 first edition. It is structured around eight core elements: governance, a heat-health warning system, populations at increased risk, communication, health system resilience, reducing heat exposure, heat-health surveillance, and monitoring, evaluation and learning. It adds user action briefs for the sectors that have to deliver, and a public health message bank so risk communication does not have to be written from scratch during a heatwave. It is written for Europe but explicitly adaptable elsewhere. WHO/Europe published it alongside the statement that Europe lost around 200,000 people to heat in four years and that nearly all those deaths were preventable.
standards.why: It is the most current, most specific and freely readable answer to what a heat plan must contain, at a moment when heat is the urban hazard with the thinnest standards coverage of any in this lane.
standards.gameEffect: Adopting it builds the heat plan as eight separate components the player funds individually, and the city's heat mortality is driven by the WEAKEST of them - a superb warning system with no cooling centres and no way to reach isolated elderly residents barely moves the death toll. Heat-health surveillance is what makes deaths visible at all: without it the city sees a hot week and no consequence, which is exactly how heat kills quietly in reality.
standards.supersedes: Heat-health action plans: guidance (WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2008)

standards.title: Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development
standards.bodyFull: World Meteorological Organization with the World Health Organization
standards.edition: WMO-No. 1142, published 2015-07-01, lead editor G.R. McGregor
standards.what: The joint WMO-WHO reference on building a heat-health warning system, written for meteorological and health services to use together. It covers who is at risk, the approaches to assessing heat stress, the science and methodology of a warning system, heat intervention strategies, risk communication, evaluation, and where the warning system sits inside a wider heat-health action plan. It is deliberately generic and non-prescriptive - it tells you what a warning system must reason about rather than what your threshold should be. It carries the practical WMO definition of a heatwave still widely used: a period of unusually hot and dry or hot and humid weather with a subtle onset and cessation, lasting at least two to three days, with a discernible impact on human activities. It came out of joint WMO-WHO work under the Global Framework for Climate Services.
standards.why: A heat warning is only useful if it is issued by the met service and acted on by the health service, and this is the document that gets those two organisations to agree on the trigger. Multi-hazard early warning coverage is also Sendai Target G.
standards.gameEffect: Builds the heat warning system, with a lead time and a threshold the player sets. A low threshold warns often, saves lives on the real events, and burns public attention so that compliance falls; a high threshold preserves credibility and misses the moderate events that actually kill the most people cumulatively. There is no correct setting, which is the point.

standards.title: Ergonomics of the thermal environment - Assessment of heat stress using the WBGT (wet bulb globe temperature) index
standards.bodyFull: International Organization for Standardization
standards.edition: Second edition, 2017-08, 18 pages; replaced ISO 7243:1989, which is cancelled
standards.what: The international method for deciding whether a person is under heat stress, and the reason outdoor work stops. WBGT combines natural wet-bulb temperature, globe (radiant) temperature and, outdoors where there is direct sun, air temperature: WBGT = 0.7 t_nw + 0.2 t_g + 0.1 t_a outdoors, and 0.7 t_nw + 0.3 t_g indoors. It is a screening method for exposure across a working day of up to 8 hours, indoors or outdoors, and it works by comparing the measured WBGT against a reference value that depends on the person's metabolic rate from the work they are doing, their clothing (via clothing adjustment values) and whether they are acclimatised. It does not apply to very short exposures. A documented limitation: its thresholds account for acclimatisation but not for other vulnerability factors.
standards.why: It is the one heat standard in this lane with an enforceable number attached to a human being rather than to a surface. It is why a construction site shuts at a given WBGT, and it captures humidity and radiant load, which an air temperature reading cannot.
standards.gameEffect: Outdoor labour productivity is driven by WBGT, not air temperature - so a humid 32 C halts work that a dry 38 C would not, and a worker in the sun beside a dark asphalt lot hits the threshold before one in a shaded street does. Construction and outdoor services slow or stop above the reference value for their work rate, which makes shade, tree canopy and high-albedo surfaces into economic infrastructure rather than decoration.

standards.title: Nature Restoration Regulation - urban ecosystems
standards.bodyFull: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
standards.edition: Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of 24 June 2024, in force 2024-08-18
standards.what: The first EU-wide nature restoration law, and Article 8 is the part that binds cities. Urban ecosystems are 22 percent of the Union's surface. Member States must ensure that by 2030-12-31 there is NO NET LOSS in the total national area of urban green space and of urban tree canopy cover in urban ecosystem areas, measured against 2024 levels - so a city that paves over a park has to replace it. From 2031-01-01 they must achieve an increasing trend in both, assessed every six years, until a satisfactory level agreed with the Commission is reached, with green integrated into buildings and infrastructure. Member States may exclude urban centres and clusters where green space already exceeds 45 percent or tree canopy already exceeds 10 percent. Be careful with the numbers in circulation: the original proposal's target of a minimum 10 percent canopy in all cities, towns and suburbs by 2050 did NOT survive into the final law - the 10 percent figure in the enacted text is an exclusion threshold, not a target. Article 13 also commits Member States to contribute to planting at least 3 billion additional trees across the Union by 2030.
standards.why: It is the only binding LAW in this lane that puts a numeric obligation on urban green space and tree canopy, which is the primary passive defence against urban heat. And the gap between the proposed 10 percent canopy target and the enacted no-net-loss rule is a clean, verifiable lesson in how an ambition becomes a floor.
standards.gameEffect: For a city in the EU, a hard planning constraint rather than a bonus: total green area and canopy area are ratcheted at their 2024 baseline, so any development that removes green must replace it somewhere in the same city before it can be approved. After 2031 the ratchet turns upward on a six-year review. Because canopy is also the strongest urban heat island lever, the constraint the player fights at first is the reason their city is survivable by mid-century.

standards.title: The 3-30-300 rule for urban forestry and greener cities
standards.bodyFull: Cecil Konijnendijk, Nature Based Solutions Institute (peer-reviewed in Journal of Forestry Research, 2023)
standards.edition: Proposed 2021; peer-reviewed as Konijnendijk, J. For. Res. 34(3):821-830 (2023), doi:10.1007/s11676-022-01523-z
standards.what: NOT a standard, and the honesty about that is the finding: it is a research-derived rule of thumb that has become a de facto benchmark because nothing standardised exists. Three thresholds: at least 3 well-established trees visible from every home, school and workplace; no less than 30 percent tree canopy cover in every neighbourhood; and no more than 300 m from every residence to the nearest public green space. Its value is that it is local and pass/fail, where conventional metrics such as city-wide canopy percentage or green space per capita average away the neighbourhoods that have none. Measurement guidance exists (Browning et al., Science of the Total Environment 907:167739, 2024, which reviews seven data types and matches them to the three components). Evidence is uneven: the 30 percent canopy component has good health evidence behind it, while the visibility and access components are less well supported. Uptake includes Indianapolis mapping it city-wide and the UN Economic Commission for Europe adopting it in its work on sustainable, healthy and resilient cities. A 2026 study of 862 European cities found under 15 percent of the studied population living in full compliance with all three criteria and 21 percent meeting none, with greenness consistently higher in wealthier settlements.
standards.why: Urban heat is the least standardised major city climate risk, and this is what fills the vacuum. Naming it as a rule of thumb rather than a standard, while still using its numbers, is the correct way to handle a field where the guidance is ahead of the standards.
standards.gameEffect: A per-neighbourhood pass/fail overlay with three lights, evaluated on the WORST neighbourhood rather than the city average - which is the whole reason to use it instead of a city-wide canopy figure. Meeting the 30 percent canopy threshold in a neighbourhood measurably drops its heat island magnitude and its WBGT for outdoor work; meeting the 300 m access threshold improves health and heat-mortality outcomes. The game should label it 'rule of thumb, not standard' on the tooltip, because it is, and because the difference between guidance and standard is a thing worth teaching.
